title: DFX Framework: Variance + Anticoncentration Strategy
content: The module header documents the Dubroff–Fox–Xu (2021) strategy for improving the basic counting bound on Erdős's distinct subset sums problem. The file is organized into four parts: (I) variance bounds (Cauchy–Schwarz and max-based), (II) anticoncentration axiom (Berry–Esseen), (III) comparison with the counting bound, and (IV) small case verifications. The key insight is treating subset sums as a random variable $X = \sum_i \varepsilon_i a_i$ and applying anticoncentration to bound how many distinct values can appear.
mathContext: The DFX bound $N \geq \sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$ beats the counting bound $N \geq (2^n-1)/n$ by a factor of $\sqrt{n}$. The counting bound only uses $|\{\text{sums}\}| = 2^n \leq N+1$ (all sums fit in $[0, nN]$). DFX additionally exploits that the sums are spread out — a Gaussian anticoncentration argument shows they cannot cluster too densely, forcing $N$ to be large enough to accommodate $2^n$ spread-out values.

title: Crude Variance Upper Bound: Σa² ≤ n·N²
content: `sum_sq_le_card_mul_max_sq` proves $\sum_{a \in A} a^2 \leq |A| \cdot N^2$ for any $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$. This is the crude upper bound on the variance $V = \sum a_i^2/4$: it bounds $V \leq n N^2/4$. The proof is a direct term-by-term comparison: each $a^2 \leq N^2$ (from $a \leq N$), so $\sum a^2 \leq \sum N^2 = n \cdot N^2$. This bound is tight only when all elements equal $N$.
mathContext: In the DFX argument: $V = \sum a_i^2/4 \leq nN^2/4$. Combined with the Berry–Esseen bound $2^n \leq C \cdot S/\sqrt{V}$ and $S \leq nN$, this gives $2^n \leq C \cdot nN / (S/(2\sqrt{n})) = 2Cn\sqrt{n}$ — a weaker bound that only gives $N \geq 2^n/(2Cn\sqrt{n})$. The improvement to $\sqrt{n}$ in the denominator requires the lower bound on $V$ from Cauchy–Schwarz.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz: (Σa)² ≤ n·Σa² (Key Variance Lower Bound)
content: `sum_sq_cauchy_schwarz` proves $(\sum_{a \in A} a)^2 \leq |A| \cdot \sum_{a \in A} a^2$ for any `Finset ℕ`. This is the QM-AM inequality (equivalently, Cauchy–Schwarz for $\langle (a_1, \ldots, a_n), (1, \ldots, 1) \rangle$). The Lean proof lifts to $\mathbb{Z}$ (where subtraction is well-defined), then uses induction on `Finset.induction_on`. The key step is that $\sum_{b \in s} (a - b)^2 \geq 0$ expands (via `ring`) to give the Cauchy–Schwarz bound, closed by `nlinarith`.
mathContext: In the DFX framework: $V = \sum a_i^2/4 \geq (\sum a_i)^2/(4n) = S^2/(4n)$. So $\sqrt{V} \geq S/(2\sqrt{n})$. Combined with the anticoncentration bound $2^n \leq C \cdot S/\sqrt{V} \leq C \cdot S \cdot 2\sqrt{n}/S = 2C\sqrt{n}$... wait — $2^n \leq C \cdot S/\sqrt{V}$ and $S \leq nN$, $\sqrt{V} \geq S/(2\sqrt{n})$ gives $2^n \leq C \cdot S \cdot 2\sqrt{n}/S = 2C\sqrt{n}$ (not quite right — the inequality direction gives $C \cdot S/\sqrt{V} \geq 2^n$, i.e. $S/\sqrt{V} \geq 2^n/C$, which with $S \leq nN$ and $S/\sqrt{V} \leq 2\sqrt{n}$ gives $2\sqrt{n} \geq 2^n/C$... This is circular. The actual chain is: $\sqrt{V} \geq S/(2\sqrt{n})$, so $S/\sqrt{V} \leq 2\sqrt{n}$. Since $2^n \leq C \cdot (A.sum + 1) / \sqrt{\sum a^2}$, we want a lower bound on the RHS, which requires $\sum a^2$ to be large — but Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\sum a^2 \geq (\sum a)^2/n$, making $\sqrt{\sum a^2} \geq \sum a / \sqrt{n}$, so $1/\sqrt{\sum a^2} \leq \sqrt{n}/\sum a$. This makes the anticoncentration bound smaller, not larger. The actual DFX argument direction: from $\sum a^2 \geq (\sum a)^2/n$ and $\sum a \leq nN$, conclude $N$ is large.

title: Sum Bounded by n·max: Σa ≤ n·N
content: `sum_le_card_mul_max` proves $\sum_{a \in A} a \leq |A| \cdot N$ for any $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$. This bounds the 'mean' of $A$: $S = \sum a_i \leq nN$. In the DFX framework, $S$ is the range of the random variable $X = \sum \varepsilon_i a_i$, so $X \in [0, S] \subseteq [0, nN]$. The proof is identical in structure to `sum_sq_le_card_mul_max_sq`: term-by-term comparison using `Finset.sum_le_sum`.
mathContext: The bound $S \leq nN$ translates to: the maximum element $\max(A) \geq S/n$ (if $\max(A) < S/n$ then each $a_i \leq \max(A) < S/n$, so $S = \sum a_i < n \cdot S/n = S$, contradiction). This is used in the DFX argument: $N \geq \max(A) \geq S/n$, and $S$ is bounded below by the anticoncentration argument.

title: Axiom: Berry-Esseen Anticoncentration (Probabilistic Frontier)
content: `anticoncentration_bound` axiomatizes the Berry–Esseen step: if $A$ has distinct subset sums and $|A| > 0$, then $2^{|A|} \leq \sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot (\sum A + 1) \cdot 2 / \sqrt{\sum a^2}$. This is the only `axiom` declaration in the file and represents the current frontier of Lean formalization. The Berry–Esseen theorem for sums of bounded independent random variables gives a quantitative normal approximation; the anticoncentration of the normal distribution then bounds how many distinct values can fit in $[0, S]$ for a distribution with variance $V$.
mathContext: The Berry–Esseen theorem: for i.i.d. zero-mean variance-1 variables $X_i$ with $\mathbb{E}[|X_i|^3] = \rho < \infty$, $\sup_x |F_n(x) - \Phi(x)| \leq C\rho/\sqrt{n}$. For subset sums $X = \sum \varepsilon_i a_i$ with $\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1/2)$: variance $V = \sum a_i^2/4$. Anticoncentration of $\mathcal{N}(S/2, V)$: at most $1/\sqrt{2\pi V}$ probability mass at any single point, so at most $S \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi V} = S\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sqrt{\sum a_i^2/4} = 2S\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sqrt{\sum a_i^2}$ points can each receive positive probability. Mathlib's `ProbabilityTheory.CLT` has the building blocks but lacks the precise quantitative form needed here.

title: DFX Lower Bound: N ≥ √(2/π)·2ⁿ/√n (1 sorry, assembles the framework)
content: `dfx_lower_bound` is the main theorem: if $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ has $n$ elements with distinct subset sums, then $2^n \leq \sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot 2 \cdot n \cdot N / \sqrt{n}$. The proof has 1 `sorry` — it needs to combine `anticoncentration_bound` with the variance bounds (`sum_sq_cauchy_schwarz`, `sum_le_card_mul_max`). The `sorry` comment says: 'Requires combining anticoncentration_bound with sum/variance bounds'. The statement is slightly weaker than the DFX bound ($\sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot 2n/\sqrt{n}$ instead of $\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sqrt{n}$) due to the non-tight constant in the axiom.
mathContext: Chain of inequalities: (1) `anticoncentration_bound` gives $2^n \leq \sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot (S+1) \cdot 2/\sqrt{\sum a^2}$; (2) `sum_sq_cauchy_schwarz` gives $\sqrt{\sum a^2} \geq \sum a/\sqrt{n}$, so $1/\sqrt{\sum a^2} \leq \sqrt{n}/\sum a$; (3) Combining: $2^n \leq 2\sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot (S+1)\sqrt{n}/S \approx 2\sqrt{2/\pi n}$... wait, this gives $N \geq 2^n\sqrt{n}/(2\sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot n \cdot N/N)$... The exact chain requires more care. The `sorry` is waiting for real-analysis manipulation of these Real-valued inequalities.

title: DFX Beats Counting Bound: n < n² (Asymptotic Improvement)
content: `dfx_improves_counting` proves $(n : \mathbb{R}) < n^2$ for $n \geq 2$, which encodes that $\sqrt{n} > 1$ and thus the DFX bound $\sim 2^n/\sqrt{n}$ is better than the counting bound $\sim 2^n/n$ by a factor of $\sqrt{n}$. The companion `improvement_factor` proves $n < n \cdot n$ for $n \geq 2$ in $\mathbb{N}$ using `omega`. Note that `dfx_improves_counting` proves the $\mathbb{R}$ version (needed for the real-number DFX bound statement), while `improvement_factor` is the $\mathbb{N}$ version.
mathContext: The asymptotic comparison: DFX gives $N \geq c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$ while counting gives $N \geq (2^n-1)/n \approx 2^n/n$. Ratio: DFX/counting $\approx cn/\sqrt{n} = c\sqrt{n} \to \infty$. For $n = 100$: ratio $\approx 10c \approx 7.98$; for $n = 10^4$: ratio $\approx 100c \approx 79.8$. The theorem $n < n^2$ is the algebraic fact underlying $1/n < 1/\sqrt{n}$ (equivalently $\sqrt{n} < n$), which holds for $n \geq 2$.

title: Small Cases: f(1)=1, f(2)=2 (Concrete Verification)
content: `f_one` proves $f(1) = 1$: the set $\{1\}$ has $2^1 = 2$ distinct subset sums ($0$ and $1$) with $\max = 1$. `f_two_max` proves $f(2) = 2$: $\{1, 2\}$ has $\max = 2$. These are the smallest cases of OEIS A005318 (the known values of $f(n)$: 1, 2, 3, 5, 11, 22, 44, 88, ...). For `f_one`, the proof manually checks the DSS condition using `Finset.subset_singleton_iff`. For `f_two_max`, the proof is trivial via `simp`.
mathContext: The known optimal sets for small $n$ are: $f(1)$: $\{1\}$; $f(2)$: $\{1, 2\}$; $f(3)$: $\{2, 3, 7\}$; $f(4)$: $\{3, 5, 6, 7\}$; $f(5)$: $\{6, 9, 11, 12, 13\}$. The DFX lower bound $\sqrt{2/\pi} \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$ gives for $n=1$: $\approx 0.798$, so $f(1) \geq 1$ ✓; for $n=2$: $\approx 1.13$, so $f(2) \geq 2$ ✓. The bound is tight up to the constant $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ vs the true constant $c \approx \sqrt{2/\pi}$ for the Conway–Guy sequence.
